title: How do I get there?
goal: Getting around town and out of town — and mastering the direction suffix *-руу / -лүү*, which differs from the place suffix *-д*.
bekal: name means of transport and ask how to get somewhere
buy a ticket, take a taxi and ask how long the trip takes

dialogs.title: Яриа — Хархорин руу
dialogs.intro: Budi wants to go to Kharkhorin, the former capital of the Mongol Empire. He asks at the bus station ticket window.

notes: ⚠️ **-руу / -лүү means "toward" and stresses direction, while -д means "at, in, to" neutrally.** *Хархорин **руу** явна* = heading toward Kharkhorin (the journey is stressed); *Хархорин**д** очно* = getting to Kharkhorin (the destination is stressed). At A1 the two can often stand in for each other — don't let this slow you down when speaking.

**The forms: -руу after back-vowel words, -рүү after front-vowel words, -луу / -лүү after words ending in -р.** *Гэр **лүү*** (to the house), *хот **руу*** (to the city), *дэлгүүр **лүү*** (to the shop).
**Юугаар вэ? = "by what?"** This is the standard question for transport, and the answer uses the *-аар* suffix you know from unit 10: *автобусаар*, *таксигаар*, *онгоцоор*, *явганаар*.
**Үдээс хойш = "after noon", үдээс өмнө = "before noon".** This is how Mongolian says a.m. and p.m. in timetables — literally the same idea as English "afternoon".
⚠️ **Автобус хүлээдэггүй is a warning to take seriously.** Long-distance buses in Mongolia leave on time and wait for no one, unlike a lot of transport elsewhere in Asia. Arrive thirty minutes early.

grammars.title: The direction suffix: -руу, -рүү, -луу, -лүү
body: This suffix is young in Mongolian — it comes from the word *уруу* (downward, toward), which fused onto the end of nouns. That's why it feels more "directional" than the old, neutral *-д* suffix.
after: ⚠️ This suffix is also used for **calling and sending**: *над **руу** залга* (call me), *чам **руу** явуулсан* (I sent it to you). In the smartphone age, this is the use you'll hear most from young Mongolians.

**For the opposite direction, use the *-аас* suffix you already know:** *хотоос* (from the city), *гэрээс* (from home), *Улаанбаатараас* (from Ulaanbaatar). The pair *-аас* and *-руу* covers the whole idea of "from … to …".

grammars.title: Asking and answering about travel
body: These four questions cover almost everything you'll need at bus stations, airports and train stations. Learn them as whole chunks, not as word order.

head: Question
Say it
Meaning
rows: How many hours is the trip?

after: ⚠️ The last two are very useful in taxis: ***Энд зогсооно уу*** to ask the driver to stop, and ***Тоолуур ажиллуулна уу*** to ask for the meter to be turned on. There aren't many official taxis in Ulaanbaatar; most "taxis" are private cars that stop when you hold out your hand, and the fare is charged per kilometer at a rate you agree on together.

**The sentence *Яаж явах вэ?* (how do I get there) is one of the most useful in any language.** It works for five hundred meters or five hundred kilometers, and you can almost always understand the answer from one word: the name of the transport.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Галт тэрэг* literally means "fire cart", and *онгоц* originally meant "boat" — Mongolian uses the word for boat for planes because both are vehicles that float. For a landlocked country, that's an interesting choice: the boat word is older than their acquaintance with the sea.

blocks.title: The horse isn't a sport — it's transport
items: Mongolia is one of the few places in the world where **horses are still everyday vehicles**, not a hobby. On the steppe, children ride horses before they can ride a bicycle.
*Морь унах* = to ride a horse. ⚠️ *Унах* means "to ride" **and** "to fall" — context tells them apart, and Mongolians find the overlap funny.
*Морьтой хүн* = a person on horseback. *Мориной уралдаан* = horse racing, one of the three events of *Наадам*.

Mongolian has more than **three hundred words** for describing horses by color, age and gait. You don't need to learn them; just know they exist, so you see how deeply the horse is rooted in this language.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Notice that **суух means both "to sit" and "to ride (a vehicle)"** — which makes sense, since taking a bus really means sitting in it. *Автобусанд суух* = to take the bus; *автобуснаас буух* = to get off the bus.

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: Does this bus go to the market?
I'm getting off at the next stop.
What time does the plane leave?

head: Place
Say it
What's there
rows: Former capital of the Mongol Empire, founded in 1220. Erdene Zuu Monastery stands on its ruins.
A national park two hours from Ulaanbaatar. The easiest place to stay in a ger.
The Gobi Desert. ⚠️ *Говь* means "stony plain", not sand desert — most of the Gobi really is rocky.
A huge freshwater lake in the north, near Siberia. You can drink the water straight from it.
The Kazakh province in the west. Home of hunting with golden eagles.
A 40-meter equestrian statue of Genghis Khan, 54 km from the capital.

blocks.text: One practical thing to know before you plan a trip: **distance in Mongolia is measured in time, not kilometers**, because most roads are unpaved. "Four hundred kilometers" can mean five hours on asphalt or twelve hours on a dirt track. If you ask *хэр хол вэ?* (how far is it), the answer will almost always be in hours.

items: Does this bus go to the market?
